topic: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016: the six steps of the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP), the bodies that act at each step (NCLT, insolvency professional, committee of creditors), who may not bid for a distressed company and why, and the time limits

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook usually opens with the Code's objectives and definitions (corporate debtor, financial and operational creditor, adjudicating authority), then lists the CIRP provisions section by section. Here the topic is cut along the life of one case: the NPA curve places the Code in the fight against bad loans, the whole six-step map is shown before any step, and then each step is zoomed into on its own canvas and the map returns with the marker one dot further. Bodies are introduced only when the case needs them (NCLT when the bank applies, the professional when the company has to be kept in shape for sale, the committee when someone must choose a plan). The eligibility rules come right after bidders appear, and their most important rule is given a story (promoters bidding back for their own company). The time limits come last, as a property of the whole map.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Follow one insolvency case through its process map, one step per canvas, and introduce each institution or rule at the step where the case first needs it.

moves.concept: IBC 2016 and CIRP as a step-by-step process
moves.what: The process is named CIRP, yaani Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process; the first step is admission of the insolvency application.

moves.concept: step 1: insolvency application to NCLT, appeal route, withdrawal
moves.what: If a bank cannot recover its loan, it can file its application with NCLT.

moves.concept: step 1: insolvency application to NCLT, appeal route, withdrawal
moves.what: NCLT, yaani National Company Law Tribunal: a statutory body set up in 2016 for the insolvency of companies and LLPs.

moves.concept: step 1: insolvency application to NCLT, appeal route, withdrawal
moves.what: It has 16 branches and the bank may apply at any of them.

moves.concept: step 1: insolvency application to NCLT, appeal route, withdrawal
moves.what: Against an NCLT order one may appeal to NCLAT, a High Court or the Supreme Court; NCLAT is unpacked as the appellate tribunal (the High Court route is doubtful).

moves.concept: step 1: insolvency application to NCLT, appeal route, withdrawal
moves.what: 'To ye thi' the first step: the application is filed with NCLT.

moves.concept: step 1: insolvency application to NCLT, appeal route, withdrawal
moves.what: After filing, the lender may withdraw its application within 30 days (a rule worth checking).

moves.concept: step 2: insolvency professional and committee of creditors
moves.what: 'Ab badhte hain next step ki or': the committee of creditors and the insolvency professional.

moves.concept: step 2: insolvency professional and committee of creditors
moves.what: Why before what: once CIRP starts the company is to be sold; before selling it must be put in decent shape so it fetches a good value; for this purpose an insolvency professional is assigned.

moves.concept: step 2: insolvency professional and committee of creditors
moves.what: The professional handles the company's affairs during CIRP and tries to maximise the value of its assets.

moves.concept: step 2: insolvency professional and committee of creditors
moves.what: The committee of creditors is everyone who lent to this company 'and whose money is stuck': the members are described by what they have at stake.

moves.concept: step 3: resolution proposers submit plans, CoC chooses by vote
moves.what: Once the professional is assigned and the committee formed, the next step starts: inviting resolution proposals.

moves.concept: step 3: resolution proposers submit plans, CoC chooses by vote
moves.what: Resolution proposers are potential investors who believe that by putting their money in they can transform ('kaaya palat') the company.

moves.concept: step 3: resolution proposers submit plans, CoC chooses by vote
moves.what: The committee must choose only one plan from all of them; if members disagree, the highest vote share decides (simplified; the Code sets a minimum vote share).

moves.concept: ineligible resolution applicants
moves.what: 'Ab yahan par ye bhi jaan lena zaroori hai': the Code sets eligibility conditions for bidders.

moves.concept: ineligible resolution applicants
moves.what: First example: an undischarged insolvent, yaani someone already declared bankrupt, cannot be a resolution applicant.

moves.concept: ineligible resolution applicants
moves.what: Also ineligible: wilful defaulters, anyone jailed for two or more years, investors whose own account has been NPA for over a year.

moves.concept: promoter misuse and the 2017 amendment
moves.what: 'Ek interesting cheez hui': owners who had not repaid their company's loans would, once CIRP began, come forward as resolution applicants and submit plans for their own company.

moves.concept: promoter misuse and the 2017 amendment
moves.what: To stop this misuse the Code was amended in 2017: no promoter may bid for his own company. Why it hurts the lenders (buying back the company cheaply after default) is left unsaid.

moves.concept: promoter misuse and the 2017 amendment
moves.what: 'To ye thi' the details of the invite-resolution-proposals step.

moves.concept: steps 4-6: NCLT approves, monitors, closes
moves.what: NCLT approves the plan the committee selected, and also monitors its full implementation.

moves.concept: steps 4-6: NCLT approves, monitors, closes
moves.what: Once the plan is implemented, the insolvency application is closed.

moves.concept: time limits: 14 days and 330 days
moves.what: The whole CIRP is time-bound: 330 days to complete; 14 days to accept or reject the application at the first step.

moves.concept: time limits: 14 days and 330 days
moves.what: 'To ye thi' the details of the Code, followed by a channel playlist plug.

narration.density: About 18 terms (IBC, CIRP, NCLT, adjudicating authority, LLP, NCLAT, insolvency application, insolvency professional, committee of creditors, financial creditor, resolution proposer/applicant, resolution plan, vote share, undischarged insolvent, wilful defaulter, NPA, promoter, time-bound) in about 320 s, about 3.4 per minute, plus five unexplained recall acronyms in the first 20 s. Brisk for a first look but steady, because the process map carries the order and each step gets its own canvas; suits UPSC revision more than a first lesson.

talmel_summary: Most changes land together with their naming word (16 of 24 tiles), because each chip, bullet or seal pops in on the word that names it; where the picture leads, it is the navigation ring moving ahead of the step's name (up to 5 s) or a bullet written early. The picture shows what is said where position carries meaning (bank to NCLT to appeal bodies; the professional placed inside the company's frame; three plans converging on the committee), but much of the rest repeats speech as text (NCLT paragraph, role notes, the ineligible list), and the strongest spoken story (promoter misuse) has no picture at all. The on-screen 10 crore loan and the NPA curve's percentages are never spoken.

voice.notes: About 180 words per minute, even and brisk, in a reading tone. Each step opens with a signpost ('ab badhte hain next step ki or', 'uske baad ... next step shuru hoti hai') and closes with 'to ye thi ...', which gives the process a clear rhythm. Acronyms are always followed by 'yaani' and the full form. Numbers are read plainly (2016, 16 branches, 30 dinon, 330 days, 14 days) and are not stressed. The one lively turn is 'ab yahan par ek interesting cheez hui' before the misuse story. The transcript reads the opening 'NPA' as 'NPS' and has a 4.5 s gap at 182-187 s.

game_ideas.player_does: Plays the lender bank whose 10 crore loan to a factory has turned NPA and pushes the case file along the six-dot CIRP board against a 330-day clock: files at an NCLT bench, appoints an insolvency professional into the factory, gathers the creditor banks into a committee, opens bidding, holds the vote, and asks NCLT to approve and monitor.
game_ideas.process_happens: At each dot the right body lights up (NCLT tags on admission, approval and monitoring); the professional's arrival stops the factory's value meter from falling; bidders' plans fly to the committee; the vote bar fills; the calendar counts down (14 days for admission, 330 in all).
game_ideas.win: A plan approved by the committee's vote and by NCLT before day 330, with the recovered amount shown back at the bank.
game_ideas.lose: Taking a step out of order (voting before the committee exists, going to NCLAT before NCLT decides) is refused; running past 330 days pushes the company towards liquidation and the bank recovers far less.
game_ideas.concept: IBC 2016 and CIRP as a step-by-step process

game_ideas.player_does: Screens bidder cards at the committee's door (a clean investor, a wilful defaulter, a person jailed three years, an investor with his own NPA account, the company's own promoter, an undischarged insolvent) and lets each in or keeps it out.
game_ideas.process_happens: Admitted bidders' plans go to the vote; a wrongly admitted one is caught at NCLT approval and the plan is struck out, losing days on the clock.
game_ideas.win: Only eligible bidders reach the vote and the plan passes NCLT first time.
game_ideas.lose: Letting the defaulting promoter in replays the misuse story: he buys back his own company cheaply, the bank's recovery meter drops, and the 2017 amendment stamp appears to explain why it is barred.

game_ideas.player_does: Drags six step chips onto the dots of an empty timeline and pins 'NCLT', 'IP' and 'CoC' tags onto the steps where each acts.
game_ideas.process_happens: Correctly placed chips lock and the ring runs along the line once all are in; each tag pinned on the right dot shows that body's action as a short animation.
game_ideas.win: All six steps in order and every tag on its step.
game_ideas.lose: A tag on the wrong step (for example the committee approving the plan instead of NCLT) shows the case bouncing back with the correct body named.

checks_learned: Every number drawn on screen (10 Cr loan, 24.8%, 2.5%, 2.78% March 2023) must be spoken, or labelled with its source and date; a current-value figure must be checked against the source for that date.
A spoken story longer than about 15 s must get its own picture (here the promoter misuse story ran 27 s over a still list).
With a process map that returns between steps, the marker must land on the step's naming word (within about 0.8 s); here it led by up to 5 s.
Legal process facts (appeal forums, withdrawal rule, vote threshold for approving a plan) must be checked against the law's text and flagged for review before narration.
Acronyms recalled from earlier lessons must each get a one-line meaning, or be dropped from the recall.
No overlay (promotion, banner) may cover the teaching diagram while a fact on it is being spoken.
When a rule exists to stop a misuse, the narration must say who loses from the misuse, not only that it was misuse.
A transcript gap of more than 4 s right after a picture change flags a line to re-check in the narration audio.

teaching_best.why: The whole process is shown as a map before any step is taught, and the voice's 'next step' signposts match the ring moving along it, so the learner never loses the thread.
The insolvency professional arrives as the answer to a reason: the company is to be sold, so it must first be kept in good shape to fetch value.
The committee of creditors is described by stake ('jinke paise atke hue hain'), which makes clear why they get to choose the plan.
A real misuse story comes before the rule that stopped it (2017 amendment), so the promoter bar has a reason.
Time limits are given last as a property of the whole process, with the calendar attached to the map.

teaching_weak.why: Five recall acronyms (SARFAESI, 5/25, SDR, S4A, AQR) in about 15 s with no meaning, over a curve whose numbers are never spoken.
NCLT is taught by reading out a definition paragraph; its role (a court that decides on insolvency) is not shown in action.
The appeal route lists a High Court beside NCLAT and the Supreme Court; this should be checked before reuse.
The 30-day withdrawal rule should be checked against the Code (withdrawal after admission is usually tied to a large creditor vote).
'Highest vote share decides' simplifies how a plan is approved; the minimum share required is not given.
The misuse story never says why promoter buy-back hurts the lenders (the company comes back to the same defaulter at a discount).
No spoken recap of the six steps and no exam link at the end.
